title: BrowseNet: Graph-based associative memory for retrieval
one_liner: BrowseNet lets a retrieval system traverse semantic relationships in a graph to find the right information, the way you browse related topics in your head.
lead: When you search a massive pile of documents for an answer, simple search engines look for exact keyword matches. BrowseNet works differently: it builds a graph where each piece of text connects to nearby pieces, then traces those connections to find information that belongs together, not just information that mentions the same words.

problem.h2: Why search breaks when ideas scatter across many documents
paras: Imagine you are looking for information about how bees talk to flowers. A simple search engine looks for pages with all three words: bees, flowers, communication. But the real knowledge is scattered. One page says bees visit flowers at dawn. Another explains how plants release scent. A third describes how insects navigate by smell. Each page has a piece, but no single page says all three together.

Traditional retrieval-augmented generation (when a language model pulls in external documents to answer questions) just ranks documents by how similar they are to your question, word-by-word. It misses the fact that a document about scent and a document about dawn visits are connected through a hidden chain: dawn timing lets insects detect fresher scent signals. The search engine has no way to follow that chain.

callout.html: Traditional search ranks documents by surface similarity but cannot traverse the hidden connections between ideas.

panels.title: 1. The mess: many documents scattered
panels.caption: Question: How do bees find flowers? A hundred documents hold pieces of the answer.

panels.title: 2. The old way: keyword search
panels.viz_args: Rank by words matched. Miss the connections.
panels.caption: Simple search finds documents with matching words, but ignores how they relate.

panels.title: 3. BrowseNet builds a graph
panels.caption: Each document chunk becomes a node. Edges connect related chunks. Darker nodes are more central to the topic.

panels.title: 4. Traverse the graph following the question
panels.viz_args: Start at a node. Jump to a neighbor. Keep following links that match the query.
panels.caption: Instead of ranking all documents at once, explore the neighborhood of related items.

panels.title: 5. Assemble the answer from the path
panels.caption: The traversed nodes together explain bees, flowers, timing, and scent as one connected story.

steps.b: Parse the document collection into chunks.
steps.text: Break unstructured text into small pieces (sentences or paragraphs). Each chunk is a node.

steps.b: Build edges from two types of similarity.
steps.text: Connect chunks that share named entities (same person, place, concept name) and chunks whose semantic content (represented as a list of numbers) is close to each other numerically.

steps.b: Convert the query to a starting point.
steps.text: Convert the question to a list of numbers (an embedding) representing its meaning. Find the chunk whose meaning-numbers are most similar.

steps.b: Traverse the graph step by step.
steps.text: From the current chunk, score neighboring chunks: how well does each match the query meaning? Jump to the highest-scoring neighbor. Repeat a fixed number of steps.

steps.b: Gather and rank the traversed chunks.
steps.text: Collect all visited chunks. Rank them by how well they match the query and where they sit in the path. Return the top chunks to the language model.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the retrieval path
paras: Most retrieval systems rank all documents at once using a single score (how similar is each one to the query). BrowseNet changes this: instead of one ranking pass, it takes a walk through the graph, visiting chunks one by one and letting each step inform the next. The walk itself—the sequence of chunks you visit—becomes the retrieval strategy.
object.object: the retrieval path (which chunks to visit and in what order)

hidden.name: How well each next step leads toward the answer
paras: At each step of the graph walk, BrowseNet computes a score for every neighboring chunk: how much does it move us closer to answering the query? This is the hidden quantity—not just whether a chunk matches the query in isolation, but whether it is a good next step given where we are now. The paper combines two signals: the chunk's semantic similarity to the query (how close its meaning-numbers are to the query's meaning-numbers) and its structural connection to the current chunk (do they share named entities, like a person or place). A high score means both things point in the same direction.

The paper estimates this score by converting the query to meaning-numbers, then at each graph position computing how similar each neighbor's meaning-numbers are to the query, plus a boost if the neighbor shares entities with the current chunk. The combination lets the walk spiral inward to coherent regions of the graph instead of jumping randomly.

heat.caption: Darker chunks have high traversal affinity for this query. Highlighted chunks form the actual path taken.

reads.html: At each step, pick the neighboring chunk that best continues the conversation toward answering your question. Prefer neighbors that share a named entity (person, place, concept) with where you are now, and also have high semantic similarity to the question.

The traversal score integrates lexical edges (named-entity overlap) with semantic edges (embedding similarity). Dynamic traversal conditions the next-step score on the current position, enabling adaptive graph exploration.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: structured search with semantic guidance
paras: A flat ranking of all documents treats the retrieval problem as independent choices: score each document separately and pick the top ones. But in reality, good retrieval is a conversation: once you find one relevant chunk, related chunks cluster nearby in the graph. By walking the graph step-by-step and using each step to guide the next, BrowseNet lets you stay in regions of the graph where information about your topic is dense. Each step reinforces the previous one.

The two-pronged scoring also prevents dead ends. If you rely only on meaning-number similarity, you might wander into a thematically close but ultimately irrelevant region—for example, drifting from bees to butterflies to insects to evolution, moving further from the original query. By also requiring named-entity overlap (shared concepts like the same plant species or geographic region), you keep connected to the original line of inquiry. The graph structure acts as a guardrail.

stages.s: Query + document chunks + graph with semantic and lexical edges
Find starting chunk closest to query embedding
Score all neighboring chunks by semantic + entity overlap
Move to highest-scoring neighbor; record the step
Repeat for fixed number of hops
Visited chunks ranked by step and relevance

math.words: At each step, the score for moving to a neighboring chunk combines how semantically close it is to the query plus a bonus if it shares a named entity with the current chunk.
math.equation: score(neighbor) = semantic_sim(neighbor, query) + entity_weight * has_shared_entity(current, neighbor)
symbols: how close the neighbor's meaning-numbers are to the query's meaning-numbers, from 0 to 1
a tunable constant (e.g. 0.2) that says how much to reward sharing a named entity
1 if the neighbor and current chunk mention the same entity (person, place, concept), else 0
the total score for that neighbor; pick the neighbor with the highest score for the next step

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Current chunk: 'Bees visit sunflowers at dawn seeking nectar.'
Neighbor A: 'Sunflowers release volatile compounds at sunrise.' (semantic_sim=0.8, shares entity 'sunflower')
Neighbor B: 'Butterflies also visit flowers for nectar.' (semantic_sim=0.7, shares entity 'flowers', not 'sunflowers')
Neighbor C: 'The monarch butterfly migrates south in autumn.' (semantic_sim=0.3, shares no entities)
Score(C) = 0.3 + 0.3 * 0 = 0.3 (lowest: far semantically + no shared entity)
Next step: jump to Neighbor A because it has the highest score.

math.note: The equation rewards both semantic closeness (staying on-topic) and entity continuity (following the thread), ensuring the walk spirals toward coherent information rather than drifting.

charts.title: Graph-based RAG baselines
charts.note: Exact match score on retrieval benchmarks. BrowseNet's adaptive walk outperforms static methods because it reuses information at each step to guide the next step, whereas static ranking treats every chunk independently without learning from earlier choices.

charts.title: Failure case: dense retrieval only
charts.note: Semantic embeddings alone (Neighbor B example) can drift off-topic. Combining structure + semantics keeps retrieval on track.

items.b: Graph construction fails if entities are not recognized.
items.html: If the named-entity extraction misses a person or place, those chunks do not link structurally. The walk loses a guardrail. For specialized domains (medical, technical), you need domain-specific entity recognizers, not generic ones.

items.b: The walk can spiral into a local cluster.
items.html: If the graph has tight cliques (many chunks all closely related to each other but distant from the rest), the traversal can get trapped, visiting the same region and missing distant-but-relevant information. This happens when entity overlap is too rewarded relative to semantic diversity.

items.b: Query embedding may not align with the graph's semantic space.
items.html: If the query is embedded using a different model than the chunks, the initial starting point can be far from true relevant regions, and early steps may go nowhere. Embedding consistency is critical.

items.b: Done right: entity extraction is domain-tuned, entity weight is balanced against semantic weight, and the embedding model is consistent across query and chunks.
items.html: Validate on a dev set that the walk avoids false-neighbor cliques and escapes local regions when they do form.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small document set (50-100 chunks) where the answer to a query is scattered: the chunks do not mention the query words directly, but do connect through shared entities and related concepts. For example, ask: 'How does colony collapse disorder affect honey production?' where one chunk discusses the disease, another discusses bee communication, a third describes how nutrient stress in colonies affects behavior, and a fourth quantifies honey yields. No single chunk says all four things. Run BrowseNet to retrieve the top 5 chunks, and verify that they form a coherent chain that answers the question. Compare against a baseline that only uses semantic similarity (no graph traversal). The demo must show that the walk follows a logical path, not a random jump.
demo.metric_eq: answerable_from_retrieved = (question can be answered using only the top-5 retrieved chunks) / (total test questions)
demo.closing: The key observation: BrowseNet's chunks often do not mention the query words at all, yet they form a connected narrative that answers the question together. Flat ranking would have missed them.
